[Of] Raymond Lully <note>original: *Raymundi Lullii*; the Latin genitive form indicating authorship by the 13th-century philosopher and mystic Ramon Llull.</note>

is [able], as much as is possible for human reason, to penetrate the secrets of Nature. In this context, it refers to the systematic application of rational principles to alchemical experiments.</note></term>; and because in such matters conjecture always aligns itself with the Art, it is therefore called "artful" <note>In the sense of being technically or skillfully constructed according to a specific method.</note>, which its powers have most clearly proven.

### I.
### Concerning the Process of the Art, and its Probability, on the side of the Matter.

Thus, the Art always originates from those things which are more certain in their nature, since the uncertain cannot be proven except from that which, at least in some way or for the most part, possesses certainty. Thus, no Art can exist unless it begins from its stated principles, some of which are material, being purified to a greater or lesser degree, and according to this [they are] nearer to or further from the <term>Work<note>The "Great Work" (Magnum Opus) or the final goal of the alchemical process.</note></term>; as for you, Dearest [Reader]! we do not wish to believe that you would be ignorant of this. Therefore, at the request of a famous King <note>Likely referring to the legendary (though debated) association between Lully and King Edward of England.</note>, in whose safekeeping and protection the very best intentions reside, so that such a great monument of philosophy or its knowledge may not be lost, we recommend this work

...[to complete] the work in the shortest manner, for the conversion of the heathens <note>original: *Heyden*; a term used historically for non-Christians. And because all intellectual labors <note>original: *Geistes-Arbeiten*; refers to works of the mind, spirit, or intellect, including the acts of reasoning and judgment.</note>—whether in action, comprehension, or judgment—cannot generally be sufficient, clearer, or more perfect according to the virtues and power [of the mind], and without being attached to comparative things (following the course and duty of Nature for the increase of the entire Christian religion and the salvation of souls), as we have demonstrated in the *Book of Questions* <note>original: *Fragebuch*; likely referring to Llull’s *Quaestiones per artem demonstrativam solubiles*, where he applies his logical system to various problems.</note>, in the 26th distinction of this Art; therefore, through this consecration <note>original: *Consecrationem*; the spiritual dedication of the alchemical process to a divine purpose.</note>, the majesty of the Royal Crown is elevated not a little. Through this, a widespread harvest for the production of many faithful mothers <note>In Llull’s philosophical system, "mothers" often refers to fundamental principles or "matrices" from which further knowledge and truths are born.</note> is publicly provided. To effect such good, the King himself is bound to us as much as possible, not by compulsion or pretense, but by his own spirit.

### 3.
### On its threefold form.

We have divided the form of our little book into three parts, according to the three classes of principles, along with all the rules of this Art. Through these—acting as its own effective instruments—the truth of the medicinal Art is illuminated, not only for the aforementioned composition but for every one handed down, showing the straightest path in the quickest manner. For everything is described according to certain grounds—not merely by contemplation but by visible proof—in the manner of the most noble demonstrable theorems. From these, the sons of logic <note>original: *Vernunftlehre*; literally the "teaching of reason." In this context, it refers to students of Llull’s logical system or "The Art."</note> will easily be able to obtain all manner of truths, especially since the subsequent and remaining fundamental teachings are proven from the first ones, as if from beginnings that depend upon the principles of this Art.

## 4.
## On the Interpretation of the Tenets, and the Distinction of the Parts.

Consequently, in mystical language <note>The "mystical language" refers to the symbolic and coded terminology (Decknamen) used by alchemists to hide their secrets from the uninitiated.</note>, we shall add an interpretation and application of each of the most prominent tenets. We will explain these—according to the prescribed method and practical order, as far as the weakness of our reason will allow—based on what our ancestors <note>The "ancestors" or "forefathers" refers to the long lineage of alchemical authorities, such as Hermes Trismegistus or Geber, whom Llull claims to follow.</note> seem to have believed regarding the matter of the principal tenets. In all these principles, however, the tenets will be divided into three parts before they are combined with those being applied; this will be demonstrated regarding the methods and titles in the following chapters.

## 5.
## On the Natural Principles of the First Genus, and Those That Flow From Them.
<note>original: *labuntur*; Latin for "to glide, slip, or flow down."</note>

Thus, the material principles <term>Material-Principia (Material Principles)</term> follow—as is customary—the very same natural matter. They do so through their own bond of love <note>In alchemical philosophy, chemical reactions and affinities were often described as "love" or "marriage" between sympathetic substances.</note>, which, through their own natural and even "loving" effects, transforms them into the metallic form, or into the very heart of it. And in this order, there are first four practical principles, of which two are natural, and the remaining two are against

nature. The natural ones are **Sulfur** and **Mercury**; and from these two, **metallic love** <note>Alchemists often used "love" or "marriage" to describe the chemical affinity and bonding between two substances.</note> is generated, through which the generation of the desired thing <note>The "desired thing" refers to the Elixir or the Philosopher's Stone.</note> occurs, where their actual individual parts are bound to one another through a natural alliance. This happens when the power of their virtue <term>Virtue (Tugend)</term> <note>In this context, "virtue" refers to the inherent medicinal or transformative power of a substance.</note> is assisted over a contrary virtue of that which is corruptible, as we shall soon reveal.

Against nature, however, are the nature of **Vitriol** and the nature of **common salt**, from which the love of the other gender <note>original: *andern Geschlechts*; likely referring to substances that are chemically dissimilar or "alien" to the metallic nature of sulfur and mercury.</note> arises, though still of a nearby generation. Among these, the corruption of the desired thing occurs—namely, insofar as their inferior nature is assisted over the better nature of the sulfur and mercury. This often happens due to the power of the superfluous clayey <note>original: *lettrichten*; referring to earthy, loamy impurities that "soil" the chemical purity of the metals.</note> mixture which overcomes the matter of the sulfur and mercury; or it happens from a lack of preparation or the ignorance of the artist.

Therefore, so that Your Royal Majesty cannot claim any cause of ignorance regarding the preparation itself, or in the future scold us in any way, we wish to grant these instructions as something very fruitful, as we have promised, in fulfillment of our word.

## 9.

### How the master should conduct himself in practice when reasoning through the fundamental doctrines.

We say to you, dearest son! that beyond physical sensation, you must lend the eyes of your intellect to serve as a guiding canon <gloss>a fundamental rule or standard</gloss> and regulation for understanding all the aforementioned fundamental doctrines. You must watch over this according to the order of the following logic <note>original: *Vernunft-Lehre*; literally "doctrine of reason," referring to the structured philosophical system used to guide alchemical experiments</note>, with a renewed memory, a diligent will, and an active intellect, if you wish to achieve the complete purpose of this work. 

However, you must pay close attention to the signs and the natures of the intermediate and extreme things <note>The "extremes" refer to the starting material and the final goal, while the "intermediates" are the transitional states or substances between them</note>, because the intermediate things are transformed into the extremes <note>original: *extremis*</note>, and the extremes are dissolved into the intermediate things. 

This cannot happen if the extreme things, according to their kind and nature, were not drawn from the intermediates—moving from potentiality into actual deed <note>original: *von der Vermögenheit in die (würckliche) That*; an Aristotelian concept where a substance has the "potential" to become something else, but requires a process to make it "actual"</note>. This is necessary because there is no direct passage from one extreme end to the other without a middle stage. This is also naturally characteristic of the imperfect metals, which appear imperfect in their kind. For this reason, all those same imperfect metals are changeable in every thing, because every intermediate thing has within itself an unformed nature; however, they will be formed and distinguished and maintained through their own extreme end-goal, which we have explained more extensively in

## Codicil

We say, however, that the extremes, insofar as they are derived from their nearest means, are easily carried out through their own inherent powers forcefully; and according to the cause of the following nature, they are (as is maintained) held back toward their own **act** <note>original: *actu*; here meaning a natural impulse or the active manifestation of a substance's potential</note>. Furthermore, my son, you must take up, one after the other, the alternating principles <note>original: *principia alternantia*</note>, which are more capable of being changed through mixing due to the proximity of nature, which is closer or more perfect in them. For example, **H.** is the beginning to obtain **G.** through the medium of **G.**, and **G.** is the principle <note>original: *principium*</note> of **M.** to reach **R.** through **M.**, and **M.** is the principle of **R.** so that it might reach **Y.** through the same, step by step, and be transformed into its nature.

And thus it is known how the nature of the extremities is recognizable through the nature of their intermediate things. Conversely, because **G.** holds the nature of the middle joining of **B.** and **M.**, and **M.** retains the means of joining the nature through which **G.** is turned into **R.**, and **R.** is by nature related to the intermediate thing through which the nature of **M.** is transformed into the nature of **Y.** 

And by **B.**, you must understand the **material principles** <note>original: *Material-Principia*</note>, namely **gold** and **silver**, and the nature of **vitriol** <term>Vitriol: a historical name for sulfate minerals (like copper or iron sulfate), used in many alchemical recipes</term> and **salt**, together with **mercury** <note>original: *mercurio*</note>.

## 13.
### Concerning the Division of this Masterpiece.

This masterpiece <note>original: "Meisterstuck." In alchemy, this refers to the "Magnum Opus" or the Great Work of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> is divided into 4 parts, according to the 4 practical principles. The first part shows how to thin the thick and coarse through smelting <note>original: "Schmelzung."</note>, the dissolution <note>original: "Auflösung."</note> of the elements, and the separation of the Stone into the 4 elements. The second part shows the manner of lightening the weighty through distilling, calcining <note>original: "calciniren." The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in order to reduce it to a powder or "ash."</note>, thickening, and burying <note>original: "egraben." Likely referring to *digestion* or *putrefaction*, where a vessel is "buried" in a warm medium such as horse dung or a sand bath to provide gentle, constant heat.</note>,

Now it is good to empty the spirits from the body—which remains on the path to its perfection—so that it may be calcined <note>original: *calcinirt*; reduced to a fine powder through high heat.</note> and mortified <note>original: *ertödet*; "killed" or stripped of its outward qualities so it can be transformed.</note>. Therefore, take it and treat it according to the operation as described in the chapters formed by **Y**.

So take then, in the name of God, the composition <note>Refers to the "matter" or "stone" that has undergone the previous stage of putrefaction/rotting.</note> that was putrefied as described above, and first distill the water entirely through the helm <term>Helm<gloss>The top part or cap of a distilling apparatus (alembic) that catches and directs the rising vapors.</gloss></term> in a **Balneo Mariae** <term>Bain-Marie<gloss>From the Latin *Balneum Mariae*, a water bath used to provide gentle, consistent heat.</gloss></term> (Water). ## 36.
## On the Separation of the Air and the Mortification of the Earth.

My son! allow the simple air with its simple fire to rise (distill) through the ashes, as they can withstand a greater heat; for it will become clear throughout the entire Practice that they withstand the simple firing. This is done because it is better that the heat and the larger earthly parts be elevated above themselves through the simple firing. Therefore, take the distilling apparatus with the entire matter and distill the air (spirit) in part, with a steady fire well-tended with sawdust <note>Sawdust was often used in alchemy to maintain a slow, consistent, and controllable smoldering heat.</note>, until you have captured all the air for this time, mixed with fire, and the fire that is hidden in the "intestines" <note>The inner core or hidden essence.</note> of the air. That which remains burnt at the bottom, however, is the fire that shall be separated from the dry and black earth.

Others have called this Earth the **Green Lion**, strong in battle. <note>The "Green Lion" usually represents a potent acidic solvent or a specific stage of mineral purification.</note> Others call it the **Swallowing Dragon**, that is, the one who freezes and **mortifies** <term>mortifies<gloss>original: "mortificiret." Others have called it a **Desolate Place**, because it is emptied of its spirits. Others call it a **Poison**, because it is deadly. Others call it the **Tree**, because it bears fruit. Others call it a **Hidden Honey**, because it is the foundation of all Nature and the governor of all elements.

Therefore, forget not, my son! This Earth, which we have named according to the letter, has mostly flowed through many and various works in the middle and the end. Because **Art** <note>The alchemist's skill and laboratory intervention.</note> always lacks its own Earth—in which the mineral virtue lies—mostly for the purpose of **hardening** <term>hardening<gloss>original: "abzuhärten." Therefore, you must freeze it with white lead or sulfur, arsenic, or mercury, through the virtuous power of its **Earth** (*Terra*) into **Sulfur** (*Sulphur*) for hardening and coloring through Art and Nature. ## 59.
## On the Investigation of the Cause Why the Second Dissolution Occurs, and What It May Be.

Now, we perform the second dissolution for two reasons. The first is so that we may have the spirits in a subtle nature, from the bodies' own substance, as a very pure water. The second cause is so that we may have the bodies, which are spongy and light by nature and robbed of their own moisture, in which the natural heat may be active, penetrating, and congealing <note>original: *gefrierende*; in this context, the alchemical process of "freezing" or fixing a volatile liquid into a stable solid.</note> its quicksilver <term>quicksilver: mercury, considered by alchemists to be the fluid, feminine principle of all matter.</term>, and transforming it into sulfur <term>sulfur: the fiery, masculine principle of metals; not necessarily the chemical element sulfur, but a "soul" or "oil" within the metal.</term>. ### 63.
## The action in the first material principles is mutual. (Reciprocal)

# Raymund Lull

...and will be naturally linked with the artificial gums after the manner of sulfur <note>original: *Schwefel*; representing the active, fiery, and masculine principle in alchemy</note>. If you understand this, my son! then you may possess the treasure of heaven and earth.

But it is necessary that at the beginning of the transformation of this water, you do not let the earth drink it in except little by little, so that it is a single swallow and not a sea; this is so that one does not become a mockery to the common folk, and so that the colors of the spirit or the **virtuous powers** <note>original: *Tugendkräften*; the inherent medicinal or transformative potencies of a substance</note> of the earth are not mutilated or killed. The first is the **passive principle** <note>original: *Satz des Leidens*; literally "the position of suffering." In early philosophy, "suffering" or "passion" refers to the capacity of matter to be acted upon or changed by an external force</note> within the essence, from whose foundation many and various tools arise out of matter, such as colors, **accidents** <term>accidents</term> <note>In Aristotelian logic, "accidents" are qualities (like color or smell) that can change without changing the fundamental nature of the substance itself</note>, and the like.

The second distinction, however, is called the "active" one, which effects the motion of contraction and expansion within the **mercurial matter** <term>mercurial matter</term> <note>The fluid, transformative principle in alchemy; the "living" silver or spirit that allows metals to grow and change</note>. Within this matter, the active force provides its impulse and preparation—or **insufflation** <note>original: *Einblasung*; the act of breathing a spiritual or vital force into a material</note>—though it can sometimes be assisted by the proportions of external things. An example of this is food; if food has not been crushed by art and well-chewed, it greatly poisons the nature of its body. And therefore, through the primary arrangement of Nature, it happens that the food is first perfectly crushed by the teeth (which are specialized for this) before it is sent to the place of **digestion** <note>original: *Däuung*</note>. It is for this reason that the contraction is narrowed or widened through a moving force, although the **Anions** <note>The "Ancients," referring to the classical Greek and Arabic authorities on alchemy and medicine</note> improperly compared it (the crushing) to the other (the digestion).

This power is twofold. Because the first is internal, and is natural to the matter, implanted by Nature, through which the matter of the metal is immediately transformed. # Codicil

...namely, before the flight <note>The "flight" refers to evaporation or sublimation, where the substance turns into vapor and escapes the vessel</note> of the mercury, and beyond this it stands until the very end; it is increased and, sinking entirely into the depths, it tints and endures.

For in a natural way, the father desires to multiply his lineage through the son, so that he may preserve in his offspring the nature which he cannot keep within himself. And thus, for this generation, he must pour forth from his own essence. ## 86.
### Concerning the Method of Fermenting Growing Things, by Way of Strengthening and the Spirit of Nature.

**W**e say, therefore, that the method of growth <note>original: *Wichsung*; here referring to the alchemical "waxing" or multiplication of the substance's power</note> is this: that the **sublimation** <term>the process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify the spirit</term> of the retained moist part is repeated so often until it performs a true **fusion** <note>original: *Schmelzung*</note> upon that same part, with its own moisture (namely, taking root and remaining, and becoming more fixed) which has never left its body through a circulated mixing. 

Also, do not think that this is the **first moisture**, as it was in its whole substance—coarse, thick, and undigested like oil or a fatty grease <note>original: *Schmehr*</note>—because it would make the **Stone** <term>the Philosopher’s Stone, the transformative goal of the alchemical Great Work</term> entirely combustible <note>alchemists sought a "non-burning" fire; if the substance contained "oily" impurities, it would simply burn up rather than transform</term>. ## On the method of practicing, and of

In the method of performing the sweetening <note>also known as "edulcoration," this refers to the process of washing away salts or impurities from a substance to make it "sweet" or pure</note> of this Stone, there is a threefold order, and also a twofold one. This is because the **fixation** <term>the process of making a volatile substance stable so that it does not evaporate or change when exposed to heat</term> and proper **melting** are accomplished either through the repetition of **dissolutions** and **coagulations**, or **sublimations**, or through a combination of both.

But for that which must be established through the **process** of **sublimation** <term>the process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, used to purify substances</term>, the wisdom of the artist must never fail to be wary of the danger. 

Therefore, regarding the method of **precipitating** <note>causing a substance to settle out of a solution as a solid</note>, it is fixed more quickly but cast more slowly. To compensate for this, one must resort to the first order; the second process is a clever invention that mixes both—namely, working both with and without **firing**.

### 93.

### Purpose of the Entire Work is Revealed.

And what has been drawn out from within it—that is, out of that same moisture—is a very subtle dryness which is bound to the moisture, so that neither one lets the other go in the subsequent distillations. At that point, all of this is called a vapor, into which the dry <term>sulfurous</term> <note>Referring to Sulfur, the active, fiery principle that gives form and color to matter.</note> element has been converted, because in that same vapor the elements are well mixed. 

When, however, the dry elements are rotated into the moist in such a manner, through many cycles of the entire moisture, then first the elements are separated from it; afterward, through other circulations which occur in the manner of transformation, the moist elements are moved into the dry. And the more these two movements are repeated, the more the earth or the <term>Stone</term> <note>original: *Lapis*; the Philosopher’s Stone, the final goal of alchemy.</note> is purified of the impure <term>Sulfur</term> and the earthly dregs that are outside of it, which come from the original mass. 

And understand well that the <term>Tincture</term> <note>A concentrated liquid essence capable of transmuting substances or healing.</note> of the month <note>original: *Monats*; likely referring to the "menstruum" or universal solvent, which is linguistically linked to the monthly cycle.</note> is separated from its coarse, dreggy earthliness through slow distillations, and is carried forth in the water of <term>Mercury</term>. Take care, therefore, that the work does not turn red before the blackness <note>In the "Great Work," the material must first turn black (the *nigredo* stage) before it can turn white and finally red. Turning red too early indicates the "flowers" or "tincture" have been burned by too much heat.</note>, and the tincture burns, which must be carried and hidden in the "belly" of the Mercury. For Mercury is its own very subtle earth, in which the fire of both the <term>Sol</term> <note>original: *Sol*; Latin for "Sun," representing gold and the masculine principle.</note> and the <term>Menstruum</term> <note>The solvent used to dissolve the solid components of the work.</note> is contained. The Solar or Lunar body <note>original: *Solar oder Lunar-Körper*; alchemical terms for gold and silver</note>, when it has been calcined <term>Calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in the air to reduce it to a fine powder</term> and transformed into oil according to our solvent <note>original: *Menstruo*; a liquid used to dissolve or extract the "essence" of a substance</note>; and know the weight of each. ### Concerning the Philosopher's Stone, one author says the following in general after much concluding.

It now remains for us to briefly recount the entire Great Work <term>Magisterium: the complete process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</term> in a short summary, so that one might almost know it by heart. Therefore, we say that the whole intention of our work, in essence, is nothing other than taking the Philosopher’s Stone and, with nimble labor and other complete processes, applying oneself to the work of sublimation <term>Sublimierung: the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifying it again to purify it</term> and distillation of the first degree. This is done so that the substance may be cleansed of the impurity of decay <note>original Latin: *corruptionis*</note>. Afterward, however, it shall be fixed <term>fixirt: a process in alchemy where a volatile, "spiritual" substance is made stable and solid so it can withstand fire without evaporating</term>, so that nothing rises upward. Once it has been fixed, dissolve what is subtle <note>In alchemy, "subtle" refers to the refined, pure essence of a material</note> from it and keep it in a moderate fire until it has been raised through the manner of sublimation, dissolution, and distillation, and can be elevated. 

When it has been elevated, keep it in a moderate fire until it is completely fixed and rests in the smoke of the fire; and this is called the second stage <note>original: *Staffel*</note> of the preparation. Indeed, herein lies the goal of preparation and perfection. Likewise, the third stage of the Stone must be administered simultaneously, in which the whole beginning, middle, and end consists of the fulfill[ment] <note>The page ends mid-word: *Erfüllung*</note>

### A Little Key (*Clavicula*) by Ramon Llull of Majorca, which is also called a Treasure Chest (*Aptorilt* <note>Likely a corruption of the Latin *Apertorium*, meaning an "opener" or manual</note>) or Master Key (*Dietrich* <note>A German term for a lock-pick or skeleton key</note>), in which everything required for the alchemical work is opened and explained.

We call this work of ours a "Key," because without this present book, no one can understand what we have written in our other books, wherein we have fulfilled the entire art—albeit with obscure words for the uninitiated. I have written many and extensive books under dark chapters and divisions, as is evident in our *Testament* <note>Referring to the *Testamentum*, a famous alchemical work attributed to Llull</note>, where we have dealt with the fundamental things of nature. There, everything that serves the Art is set down, yet "under the hammer" <note>likely meaning forged or refined through difficult practical labor</note> in the first text of <term>Philosophy</term> <note>original: *Weltweisheit*, literally "World-wisdom"</note>. Likewise, [it is set down] in our chapter on the <term>Philosophers’ Mercury</term> <note>Not common quicksilver, but a purified "spirit" or "mercury" of the metals</note>, and in the second part of the *Testament* concerning the abundance of the physical ore-mines, and in our book on the first <term>Quintessence</term> <note>The "fifth essence," a highly purified and potent extract of a substance</note>.

<keywords>Ramon Llull, Clavicula, Alchemical Key, Philosophers' Mercury, Quintessence, Alchemy, Testamentum, Majorca</keywords>

Likewise, concerning the <term>Quintessence</term> <note>The "fifth essence," a highly purified and potent extract of a substance</note> of Gold and Silver, [this is treated] hereafter in other books that have been made by me, wherein the entire Art is complete. We have hidden the secret to the best of our ability.

Furthermore, because without this secret no one can penetrate into the mines (<note>original: *Mineras*</note> <note>Referring here to the "ores" or "mines" of the philosophers, the source materials for alchemy</note>) of the <term>Philosophers</term> <note>original: *Weltweisen*, literally "world-wise"</note>, nor do anything that might be useful to him; therefore, with the help of the Highest—whom it pleased to reveal this secret to us—I will explain the whole Art without any fabrication. And therefore, take care not to reveal this secret to the ungodly, but only to your most faithful friends, because you are not obliged to give it to anyone, since it is a gift from God, who will give it to whom He wills. Whoever possesses this shall have an eternal treasure. Thus, recognize how to improve the imperfect through the perfect. Gold (<note>original: *Sol*, the Sun</note>) is the father of all metals, and Silver (<note>original: *Luna*, the Moon</note>) is the mother, although the Moon receives its clarity from the Sun. ### Chapter 6.
## Transformation of the Living Lime into True Silver (the Moon).

If you now have a large quantity of **living lime** <term>Kalch: the powdery residue or "ash" left after a metal or mineral has been heated to extreme temperatures</term>, or of our **ore** <gloss>mineræ</gloss>, then take an uncovered **crucible** <term>Tiegel: a heat-resistant container used for melting metals</term>, and put into it one **ounce** <note>original: ʒ; likely an apothecary's symbol for weight</note> of pure silver; and when it is melted, add over it four ounces of your powder in **pills** <note>small, hand-rolled pellets of the alchemical substance</note>. ### Chapter 15.

# LAWRENCE VENTURA
## VENETIAN DOCTOR OF MEDICINE,
### BOOK ONE,
### CONCERNING
# THE PHILOSOPHERS' STONE.

->That the Art of Alchemy is True.<-

## Chapter I.

Many believe the art of alchemy <note>original: *Alchymey*</note> is not true, to which they are moved by two reasons: First, because Aristotle in Book 4 of the *Meteorology* <note>Aristotle's *Meteorologica*, a foundational text for medieval and Renaissance science.</note> says: The practitioners of alchemy should know that the forms <term>the essential nature or "species"</term> of metals cannot be changed. Secondly, because they see that all laborers in this art make nothing but pure sophistical <term>deceptive or imitation</term> transmutations, and no one performs any true ones. Therefore, they believe that since they see it done by no one, it cannot be done correctly and truly. But neither of these two [reasons]

<summary>This page introduces Laurentius Ventura's defense of alchemy, addressing two primary skeptical arguments: Aristotle’s scientific objections and the failure of contemporary alchemists to produce genuine results.</summary>
<keywords>Lawrence Ventura, alchemy, Philosophers' Stone, Aristotle, Meteorology, transmutation, metallic species, skepticism</keywords>

--- Page 248 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument from page 219, where the author began refuting the two main objections to alchemy. The text picks up from the sentence: "But neither of these two [reasons]..."</meta>

<page-num>220</page-num>
<header>Lawrence Ventura</header>

...from these two [reasons], it follows necessarily that this glorious and excellent Art should not, for that reason, be true. For the first argument of the adversaries has no standing, even though it is true—as Alphidius <note>An Arabic alchemical authority frequently cited in medieval texts.</note> and the *Rosarius Major* <note>original: *Rosarius Major*; likely referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum* or "Rose Garden of the Philosophers," a seminal alchemical treatise.</note> say—that the forms <term>the essential, defining nature of a species</term> of things cannot be changed. However, the individuals <note>original: *individua*; the specific, physical instances of a category</note> of certain forms can indeed be changed into one another.

And this is proven by visual evidence, especially in those things that share one or two qualities with each other, as can be seen in the elements: and thus, stone is made from earth, and ash from wood, and from ash and stones, glass is made, etc. It happens similarly with metals, because all metals have in common a single matter, which is quicksilver <note>original: *argentum vivum*</note> with its sulfur <note>original: *Sulphur*</note>.

And the metals are distinguished only by more or less cooking <term>coction; the natural or artificial process of maturing metals within the earth through heat</term>, which occurs through the ripeness of their sulfur by means of this cooking. For sulfur is the form of metals, and especially of gold—not indeed common sulfur, but the transformed kind, as Master Bonus <note>original: *M. Bonus*; Petrus Bonus of Ferrara, a famous 14th-century alchemical author.</note> says. ### Of the Philosophers' Stone. <note>original: *De Lapide Philosophorum*</note>

That it is indeed true that metals cannot be changed by any kind of skill or method, unless they are first brought back into their **first matter** <term>materia; the fundamental substance or "prime matter" from which all things are composed</term>.

The first **matter** of all metals, however, is **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum; the liquid metal mercury, considered a foundational element in alchemy</term> and **sulfur** <term>sulphur; in alchemy, the active, combustible principle, not necessarily the common chemical element</term>—not indeed in their [common] nature, but transformed, that is, turned into a steam. And thus the first **matter** of metals is a moist, dirty steam or **vapor** <term>vapor; a gas or steam produced through heating</term>, which encompasses within itself the nature of both **quicksilver** and **sulfur**.

From this, it now necessarily follows that if, through Art, such an **oily vapor** <term>vapor unctuosus; a "greasy" or dense steam believed to be the seed of metals</term>—or dirty steam—can be drawn out of those things in which it resides, and if it is found to be identical to that which **generates** <term>generates; the natural process of creation or growth within the earth</term> the metals in the **ores** <term>minera; the natural veins or source materials of minerals in the earth</term> of the earth: then a **Medicine** <term>medicina; another name for the Philosophers' Stone or Elixir, capable of "healing" base metals into gold</term> can also be made. This Medicine, when cast over simple, imperfect bodies and **quicksilver**, can change them into a true and perfect metallic **body** <term>corpus; the physical substance or metallic form</term>, which will be much more perfect than all natural metals.

It is also to be known, however, that this **Medicine** is drawn from some things more easily and abundantly, but from others with more difficulty and imperfection, whether they be the metals themselves or whatever other things they may be. This, however, cannot happen unless such things are first destroyed through **putrefaction** <term>putrefactio; the stage of rotting or breaking down matter to release its essence</term> and decay, until they receive another, nobler form through proper boiling and long **digestion** <term>digestio; a process of slow, constant heating intended to mature or refine a substance</term>.

### On the Stone of the Philosophers.
<note>original Latin header: *De Lapide Philosophorum*</note>

Therefore, Nature, from the source or beginning, has mixed the two aforementioned **principles** <term>Principia; the fundamental components of all things, in this case, Sulphur and Mercury</term> in certain measures and weights with filth and impurity within their minerals. Instead, it acts only upon the Mercury, as upon a thing that is disposed to be acted upon, and thus it changes that which is changeable and separates the pure from the impure.

...be reduced. Therefore, the **First Matter** <term>erste Materi; the primary, formless substance from which all things are created</term> is understood as that which has no form at all. One cannot give it a new form unless it is first destroyed: and in the generation of things, the process and progression from the first matter to the final state occurs through various intermediate forms. Therefore, this must also happen in the destruction, for the birth of one thing is the destruction of another.

And thus metals are reduced into their first matter when they are brought back to that same first simplicity and oneness which their elements possessed in their first composition. In this state, they were truly **spirits** <note>original: *Spiritus*</note> and **vapors** <note>original: *Vapores*</note>, or steams, which are made perfect by nature into a composite form. For nature, as Master Bonus <note>Petrus Bonus, a 14th-century Italian alchemist and author of 'The New Precious Pearl'</note> says, generates the Medicine from the very same or entirely identical beginnings from which nature gives birth to metals. This thing from which the Medicine is drawn must also be composed of its elements in proper number, weight, and measure; it must also be put together by nature with such proportion that it is entirely uniform with the nature of the metals and is of the best possible **temperament** <term>complexioniert; the balanced state of the four primary qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry)</term>.

## Chapter 4.
# That it is granted to the **Philosophers** alone to know and to make this **Medicine**.

Since it was stated above that the **Philosophers** <term>Philosophen; referring here specifically to "True Alchemists" who seek natural secrets</term> possessed this **Art**, for they all speak of the **Philosopher’s Stone** <term>Lapide Philosophorum; the legendary substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold</term> and write wonderfully about it: we must therefore see whether they obtained the same through their own understanding, or rather through divine assistance. To know this, one must understand that there are two things that make the **Art** difficult: namely, discovering the **Matter** <term>Materi; the raw starting material or "prime matter"</term> from which the **Elixir** is made; and then also its **Regimen** <term>Regiment; the specific sequence of operations, heating, and timing required</term>.

For in such a vast multitude and variety of things, it is very difficult to recognize which thing is suitable for this work and is closest to the nature of the **metals**. It is, however, much more difficult to recognize and to know which method of working is the most powerful. Just as it was more difficult to recognize from which **Principles** <note>original: "Principiis"</note> and beginnings the **metals** are generated, than by what order and how they are **perfected** <term>perficiert; the process of refining a "sick" metal like lead into "healthy" gold</term>; and yet they discovered both through their skill and investigation.

Regarding the first, **M. Bonus** <note>Petrus Bonus (Master Bonus), a 14th-century alchemist from Ferrara, author of the *Pretiosa Margarita Novella*</note> says in chapter 6: The knowledge of the **Matter** is no small gift to those who desire to come to the **Art**. For it is this which the **Philosophers** sought beforehand, so that they might arrive at the knowledge of the **Form**.

For that same **quicksilver** contains within itself the aforementioned essential and specific sulfur. Indeed, every **sulfur**, or anything that possesses the nature of sulfur, has the property of coagulating **quicksilver**.

From this, it is understood that the **Philosophers** possessed both: a certain and specific **matter**, and also the specific **mastery** <term>Magisterium; the complete alchemical process or "The Great Work"</term> and **governance** <term>Regiment; the precise control of heat, timing, and sequence in the laboratory</term> of the same. ...and transform [it] into a true essence of an **elixir** <note>The Elixir or "Medicine," often synonymous with the Philosopher's Stone, capable of transmuting metals or healing the body</note>. Therefore, although the **philosophers** <note>The "Sages" or historical alchemical authorities</note> through their understanding, effort, and labor have discovered both the **matter** <term>Matter; the raw material or "prima materia" used to begin the Great Work</term> and the **regimen** <term>Regimen; the prescribed method, timing, and sequence of chemical operations</term>: one should nonetheless say that they possessed all such things through both divine revelation and inspiration. For **God**, who is the first cause, creator, and ruler of all things, has through His wisdom and goodness bestowed various gifts upon different people, according to the opportunity of time and place, as it seemed good and useful to Him for those to whom He gave them. 

Which is true not only of spiritual gifts, which concern souls and virtues: but also of temporal ones, which belong to the bodies themselves, or even to external things, such as wealth, honor, health, strength, and the art of handicrafts. But among all other arts, this [alchemy] is the most excellent: firstly, because of its philosophical utility, for it is closest to philosophy. Next, because of the ease of the work. For one does not need to work long or hard <note>This refers to the common alchemical claim that once the "Secret" is known, the work is "as easy as the play of children."</note>. Thirdly, because of the immeasurable utility and fruit. For countless goods follow thereafter.

This **stone** is also nobler and more wondrous than all others, because it [is] not [given] to every...

# On the Philosophers’ Stone.

Here *Lilium* <note>original: *Lilium*; likely referring to the *Lilium Intelligentiae* or *Lilium inter Spinas*, popular titles for alchemical treatises</note> says: It is a single thing, which has within itself a *Body* <note>original: *Corpus*</note>, which tinges <note>original: *tingiert*; refers to the alchemical power to "dye" or transform the color and nature of a substance</note> simultaneously with the spirit and the soul, in whose operation no other helper is necessary; under which figure the prophet *Ezekiel* saw one wheel within another wheel, and a spirit of life which was in the midst of the wheels. Thirdly, this stone encompasses four things within itself. # On the Philosopher’s Stone

Generation and birth come from the most proximate beginnings, as is evident from the seventh book of the *Metaphysics* <note>original: *Metaphysicorum*; a reference to Aristotle’s work exploring the nature of existence and substance</note>. Just as the two spirits <note>original: *Spiritus*</note> of nature—namely **Sulfur** and **Mercury**—are bodies in potentiality <note>original: *potestate corpora*; meaning they have the capacity to become solid matter but have not yet fully manifested as such</note>, for they are the principles <note>original: *Principia*</note> and elements <note>original: *Elementa*</note> of the metals; and conversely, they are so materially <note>original: *Materialiter*</note> and formally <note>original: *Formaliter*</note>, as is evident in their ores.

For from these spirits alone, nature makes bodies in actuality <note>original: *Actu corpora*</note>, and vice versa. Not that she mixes the bodies with spirits so that the spirits are converted into the bodies. Likewise, Art <note>in this context, "Art" refers to the practice of alchemy as a refined imitation of nature</note> also generates an **Elixir** from the most proximate principles and beginnings, from which gold is generated; for the Elixir is the most proximate form of gold. Or, the principles of gold <note>original: *Principia auri*</note> are only these two spirits: Sulfur and Mercury. Likewise, nature makes stable bodies—namely gold—solely from these same spirits without the addition of any other body. This happens so that such spirits, through suitable cooking <note>original: *Kochung*; the alchemical process of prolonged, controlled heating intended to mature a substance</note>, take on the property, nature, and essence of a body, and become stable solely out of themselves. Therefore, Art also makes a stable Elixir in the fire solely from these same spirits.

And just as the mineral spirits are not common but altered, so also are the spirits of Art. And just as nature makes bodies in actuality <note>original: *actu Corpora*</note> solely from these spirits, namely from the spirits which are bodies in potentiality <note>original: *Potestate corpora*</note>:

### That many who seek the *Stone* <note>original Latin: *Lapidem*</note> cannot find it, but rather wander in error.

Some, however, have also added arsenic to this; some have added marcasite <term>Marcasit: a mineral, often iron pyrite or "fool's gold," used in alchemical experiments</term>, or calamine <term>Galmey: a zinc ore</term>, or antimony <term>Antimonio: a brittle, silvery metalloid</term>, or other minerals, and labored upon them.

Others have applied their work to animal and vegetable substances: and all have come to shame because of two deficiencies—namely, the lack of suitable material and proper operation. For they have not rightly considered the specific and most immediate principles <note>original Latin: *Principiis*</note>, of which there are three—namely, mercury <term>Argentum vivum: literally "living silver," the fluid or passive principle</term> and sulfur <term>Sulphur: the "soul" or active, combustible principle</term>, though in a transformed state—and the proper measure and proportion mixed by nature. They have also failed to consider the mineral boiling heat and the virtue <note>original: *Tugend*; here meaning the inherent power or property</note> of the place (which is the beginning of generation) impressed upon the heavenly bodies. Each of these factors, by itself, introduces an inequality in the birth of metals; but much more so when all are acting together. 

From the first <note>referring to the three principles mentioned above</note> follows the contrariety <note>original: *Widerwärtigkeit*; the opposing or conflicting nature</note> of the elements, or rather of the elementated things from which the metals are generated. From the second <note>referring to the proportion and measure</note> follows the inequality of perfection and completeness: for from an unequal digestion and cooking <note>original: *Kochung*; the natural or artificial heating process that matures a substance</note>, the purer and impurer elements of the metals are generated and mixed, and the mixed elements are united. From the third <note>referring to the heat and celestial influence of the "place"</note>, the various forms of the metals and minerals are born.

# Laurentius Ventura

Therefore, although metals and marcasites <term>Marcasite: a term often used in old chemistry for iron pyrites or "fool's gold," though here it refers more broadly to mineral ores that share the traits of metals</term> share these two principles <note>original Latin: *Principia*</note> in common—namely, sulfur <note>original: *Sulphur*</note> and mercury <note>original: *Mercurium*</note>—the proportion, mixing, and digestion <term>Digestion: the process of slow, steady heating or maturation, likened to how the body processes food</term> are very unequal in these different things. For this inequality of mixing and digestion is the cause of the variation that the matter suffers in many ways. Thus, these very same qualities <note>original: *Qualitates*</note> of the elements <note>original: *Elementen*</note> are present in simple things as well as in those that are joined together.

Therefore, the metals unite with one another in their common passions <term>Passions: in this context, the inherent properties or the ways a substance is acted upon by external forces</term>, because they desire only a final form. 

But marcasite, or sulfur, or mercury, in their own nature, are the beginnings from which the metals are composed <note>original: *componirt*</note> and put together. Rather, a third nature—mixed in the correct measure <note>original: *Mensur*</note>—is born from them. Otherwise, Nature could not bring them together in one place to fulfill their generation <note>original: *Generation*</note>. For neither the nature of minerals nor that of plants <note>original: *Vegetabilien*</note> possesses the local motion <term>Local motion: the physical ability to move from one place to another; Ventura argues that minerals cannot move themselves to find their perfect partners, so the alchemist must do it</term> necessary for generation.

But Art <note>The "Art" refers to Alchemy</note> possesses both of these in the acts of separation and joining. Therefore, this "third nature" must possess a common nature within itself, which is changed from the nature of those things that compose it; and it must come from their various mixings and digestion. And within this third nature lies the mineral virtue <note>original: *Tugend Mineralis*; "virtue" here refers to an inherent power or specific property</note> to generate a composite substance <note>original: *Compositum*</note>.

# On the Philosophers' Stone

Of **composites** <note>original Latin: *Compositorum*</note> or composed things, however, there are two kinds: The first is that where the composing ingredients are set entirely as the **matter** <note>original: *Materi*</note>, and from this **composition** a new **form** arises which is unlike the forms of its simple components. However, there does not remain within them the power for further metallic **form** that could be achieved through the **digestion** <term>Digestion: the alchemical process of maturation or "cooking" through steady heat, modeled on how a stomach processes food or how a womb develops an embryo</term> of nature. Such things are **marcasites** <term>Marcasite: a general term for various metallic ores, often iron pyrites</term>, **vitriols** <term>Attramenta: literally "blackings," usually referring to vitriols or metallic sulfates used to make ink</term>, and **magnesia** <term>Magnesia: in alchemy, this refers to a variety of mineral "mother" substances thought to contain the seeds of metals</term>.

However, there are other **composites** where the composing ingredients are not set entirely as the **matter**; rather, one acts as the active force <note>original: *würkende*</note> and the other as the **matter**. These do not remain under the same **form** in which the **components** or composing things existed in their first arrangement. Moreover, through their mutual acting and suffering <term>Passion: from the Latin *pati*, meaning to be acted upon; the passive state of the material as it is transformed by the active force</term>, they can be cooked and changed from one **form** to another until they attain the final **form** and **perfection**, which is the **form** of gold. At that point, the **agent** <note>original Latin: *Agens*</note> or active force is separated from the **matter**.

And such cooking and **digestion** occurs in the **generation** of metals, the **matter** of which is mixed from two **principles** <note>original: *Principiis*</note> in the mines—namely, **sulfur** <note>original: *Sulphure*</note> and **mercury** <note>original: *Mercurio*</note>. It does not remain under the **form** in which it existed in its first composition, but rather one constantly acts and the other is acted upon until a new **form** is born—namely, an imperfect metal—and even then, the **agent** or active force has not yet been separated from the **matter**:

There, the hour of birth is noted and recognized.

### On the Philosophers' Stone.

No matter how much it is purified through **sublimation** <term>Sublimation: A process where a solid is heated into a vapor and then condensed back into a purified solid, skipping the liquid phase</term>, it still cannot be of the same composition and substance as gold. Nor can it be taken as the **matter** <note>In alchemy, "matter" is the passive substance that receives a "form"</note> itself; for no **active agent** <note>original: *Agens*</note> is ever categorized as the matter. Furthermore, because **Sulfur** <note>original: *Sulphur*</note> alone possesses no matter upon which it might act through constant cooking, it cannot finally extract a **form** from the **potentiality of matter** <note>original: *de potentia materiæ*; the philosophical idea that matter has the "potential" to become something else once the right force is applied</note>. If this could happen, it would surely be seen in the **ore** <note>original: *Minera*</note>, where it would be brought to the perfection of the **Medicine** <term>Medicine: Another name for the Philosophers' Stone, believed to "heal" base metals into gold</term>. After mixing with **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurio*</note>, it would quickly **coagulate** <note>Solidify</note> into a metal—which simply does not happen.

Thirdly, since Sulfur cannot be made stable—unless one **calcines** <term>Calcine: To reduce a substance to powder by heating it to high temperatures</term> it, and it can only be calcined through sublimation, both of which are extremely difficult because it is so flammable—it is even harder to **tinge** <term>Tinge: To transform the color and internal nature of a metal, a key step in transmutation</term> it with a perfect Medicine. It is entirely impossible to make it brilliant and shining, as the **Elixir** requires.

Others, however, who labor only with **quicksilver** <note>original: *Argento vivo*</note>, err even more, as **Aldimarus** <note>Likely a reference to a medieval alchemical authority</note> says. They first sublimate it and then, over eighty days, **fix** <term>Fix: To turn a volatile or liquid substance into a stable solid that can withstand heat</term> it with a gentle fire until it gains a metallic flow. But this Medicine is in vain, as it consists only of a **passive matter** without an **active Sulfur**, and thus cannot be made perfect...

# Laurentius Ventura
<note>Laurentius Ventura was a 16th-century Venetian physician and alchemist known for his work "On the Rational Method of Compounding the Philosophical Stone."</note>

For this reason alone, **gold** is entirely deprived of **Sulfur** <note>original: "Sulphuris"</note> after the completion of the **cooking** <term>Kochung</term> <note>In alchemy, "cooking" or digestion refers to the prolonged application of steady heat to mature a substance.</note>, and because of this, it is also more indestructible and more stable than all other metals.

And even though the **Sulfur** in the beginning starts to **coagulate** <term>coagulieren</term> <note>To turn a liquid or volatile substance into a solid.</note> the **quicksilver** <term>Argentum vivum</term> <note>Literally "living silver," the traditional name for mercury.</note> and to **tinge** <term>tingieren</term> <note>To "tinge" means to transform the color and internal nature of a base metal into a noble one.</note> it with various colors: yet after long cooking, the **quicksilver** possesses within itself the power to coagulate and to tinge without another **Sulfur**, or with very little **Sulfur**.

For both **tinctures** <term>Tincturen</term>, white and red, come from the two **spirits** <note>original: "Spiritibus"; likely referring to the volatile principles of Mercury and Sulfur.</note>: yet the white is essentially from the **Mercury**, whereas the redness is essentially from the **Sulfur**. Therefore, since the **Mercury** has taken the virtue and substance of the **elixir** in the **coagulation** and cooking from the **Sulfur**: it will also take from it the power to color and to change every **body** <term>Corpus</term> <note>The "body" refers to the solid metallic base being acted upon by the alchemical agent.</note> into a **perfect** metal—and first into a white [metal] in the first cooking, and thereafter into a red [metal] in the final cooking. Thus, the first tincture is from the **Mercury**, which it takes unto itself from the cooking **Sulfur**. The sign of this is that every metal, when it is purified, shows outwardly more of the nature of **coagulated mercury** <note>original: "Mercurii coagulati"</note> than of a **Sulfur**, because of its external abundance.

### On the Philosophers' Stone.

...was in potential <note>original: "potestate"; referring to a power or state that exists but is not yet physically active.</note>, reduced into a volatile state in act <note>original: "actu"; meaning it has now been physically realized or put into motion</note>, it retains the volatile property. Therefore Geber <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, the 8th-century "Father of Chemistry."</note> says: When the quantity <note>original: "Zahl"</note> of the volatile exceeds the quantity of the fixed, it flees away with it. But if the sum of the fixed exceeds the sum of the volatile, they both become stable <note>original: "beständig"</note> at the same time. It is evident, however, that when the fixed exceeds the volatile, it brings the work to perfection. But if the volatile exceeds the fixed, it ruins the work and brings it to nothing. Therefore it is said in the *Turba* <note>The *Turba Philosophorum*, or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, written as a dialogue between sages.</note>: Wage a war between the ore and the mercury <note>original: "Mercurio"</note>, etc. To wage a war is the same as to destroy it—namely, at the time when they wish to become united again after the war—and that is, the Sun <term>Sol</term> and Moon <term>Luna</term>, Sulfur <term>Sulphur</term> and Mercury <term>Mercurius</term> <note>These represent Gold, Silver, and the two fundamental alchemical principles of fire/stability and liquidity/transformation.</note>. In which one must so often make the volatile fixed, and conversely, until they become stable together and flow, with transformation, into true Gold and Silver. And this quicksilver <term>Argentum vivum</term> is wedded to the gold and vice-versa <note>original: "& contrà"</note>, according to the philosophers. And because a single substance is the subject <term>Subjectum</term> of both the fixed and the volatile, it is possible for the fixed to rise with the volatile, and conversely, for the volatile to be made stable with the fixed. And all this happens in one vessel without the rubbing of hands <note>This implies the reaction occurs through heat and internal chemical "sympathy" rather than manual labor like grinding in a mortar.</note>. From this it is evident that the Stone is properly called Mercury <term>Mercurius</term>, even though it is also called "gold of the philosophers" <term>aurum Philosophorum</term>—having been drawn out of the Mercury—and by many other countless names besides.

### Chapter 15.

## That a Suitable Vessel is Required for the Regimen.

There is also something else necessary for the <term>regimen</term> <note>original: "Regiment"; the "governance" or controlled management of the chemical process, specifically the regulation of heat over time</note> and the preparation of the Stone: namely, a suitable vessel. ### Chapter 17.

## That Sealing is Necessary for the Governance. <note>In alchemy, "governance" or "regiment" refers to the controlled management of heat and conditions over time.</note>

However, the vessel must not only be very strong; it must also be well sealed, as has been said. For if the most subtle **spirits** <note>original: "Spiritus" — the volatile vapors or essences released during heating</note> were not retained, the entire work would be ruined. For as soon as the stone is placed into the vessel, it begins to sweat because of the narrowness of its prison, and the most subtle parts begin to rise. The longer it is cooked, the more the **spirits** are increased, refined, and strengthened. ### Chapter 18.

## That the furnace, which is called the Athanor, is necessary.

The furnace in which one places the vessel with the material and cooks it must be no less suitable than the vessel itself. For it was said above that the entire governance of our **Mastery** <term>Magisterium: The successful completion of the alchemical Great Work</term> and our work depends upon the fire, the vessel, and the sealing. For without these, our Mastery cannot be accomplished, as is expressly stated in the *Book of Saturn* <note>original: *lib. Saturni*; likely referring to a treatise on lead or the slow, foundational stages of alchemy</note>: A proper fire certainly cannot be applied unless the furnace is prepared and suitable for it.

Therefore, an artist must (according to the saying of Morienus <note>Morienus Romanus: A legendary 7th-century alchemist and hermit known as the teacher of Prince Khalid ibn Yazid</note>) understand the quality of the fire and his furnace, as well as the rising of the fire—namely, in which part of the furnace or in which place the fire should be lit. Regarding this, three things are to be noted: First, a correct disposition of the furnace; second, a convenient proportion of the fire, so that it is neither too large nor too small, neither too high nor too suppressed; and third, that the walls are neither too thick nor too thin. Rather, it should be made so that it accepts, retains, and provides a sufficient and steady warmth.

For a large furnace or a small one, as well as a thin or a thick one, are not heated with equal and steady warmth. Therefore Morienus says:

## Chapter 19.

->That in our process no other work is performed by hand, but by fire alone.<-

It has already been stated that fire is necessary in our Mastery of the Stone <term>original: *Magisterio Lapidis*; the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</term>. However, it has not yet been explained whether other actions belong to it, such as calcination <note>reducing a substance to powder through dry heat</note>, sublimation <note>the process where a solid turns into vapor and then back to solid</note>, distillation, the separation of the elements, incineration <note>burning a substance to ash</note>, and other such operations which are said to occur in the governance of the Stone <term>original: *regimine Lapidis*; the regulated sequence of alchemical steps</term>. Furthermore, many repetitions, weights, and different times are mentioned. But if anyone looks closely at the books of the Philosophers <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers specifically to alchemical authorities</note>, they will find that in this Mastery there is only a single operation and preparation <note>original: *Confection*</note>; all the other operations they speak of are handled and completed through fire alone. For Master Bonus <note>likely Petrus Bonus, a 14th-century alchemist and author of the *Precious Pearl*</note> says in Chapter 2: They all agree that there is a single certain time of cooking to complete the white and red Elixir <note>The white elixir was believed to transmute metals into silver, the red into gold</note>. Although they sometimes change and interrupt the time in their teachings, they do this so that they might lead the Sophists <note>a derogatory term for false alchemists or "puffers" who followed recipes literally without understanding the underlying principles</note> into error.

And Hamis <note>likely an Arabic alchemical source, possibly Ibn Umayl</note> says: The Philosophers say many things that they themselves do not do. For there is one way and one thing; therefore, you need not with the...

But after the departure of the blackness toward the lemon-red color, they call it gold. But when it is from the last, it is called a *theriac* <note>original: *Tiriac*; historically a "universal" medicinal potion or antidote</note> or a tingeing poison <note>a "poison" in alchemy often refers to a substance so potent it "infects" or transforms everything it touches</note>.

In the same place: The Sages have composed their books in a figurative way, so that they might blind the unwise. But I tell the wise that there is one work, one way, one thing, one governance <note>original: *Regiment*; the controlled sequence of heat and chemical changes</note>, the effect of which is the transformation of nature—namely, a wondrous mixing of the warm with the cold, and the moist with the dry. Therefore *Mireris* <note>a speaker in the *Turba Philosophorum*</note> and many others in the *Assembly of the Philosophers* <note>original: *Turba*; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> say: The whole work is completed with a single *disposition* <note>original: *Disposition*; arrangement or preparation</note>, from which, as if from a root, each thing takes its power and tincture. But the Philosopher has divided the work when he says: Cook, grind, repeat, and do not let it weary you, and see to it that you do not err. For mixing, cooking, sublimating, roasting, calcinating <note>reducing to powder by heat</note>, whitening, grinding, watering, and tingeing are many names for a single

<page-num>329</page-num>

# On the Philosophers' Stone.

<sig>X 5</sig>

<meta>catchword: The</meta>

Invert the elements, and you will find what you seek. But to "invert" the **elements** <note>original: *Elementa*</note> means to make the moist dry and the volatile fixed <note>original: *beständig*; in alchemy, a "fixed" substance is one that can withstand fire without evaporating</note>. Once you have accomplished this, let it remain in the fire until the **body** <note>original: *Corpus*</note> is transformed into a **spirit** <note>original: *Spiritum*</note> and remains a thin and tingeing substance. And **Rhazes** <note>original: *Rasis*; referring to the 9th-century Persian alchemist and physician al-Razi</note> says in the third book of his *Words*: That same **spirit** <note>original: *Spiritus*</note> is turned into a body, and then a union is formed between the cold and moist, and between the warm and dry. And this occurs through the power of God, and through the temperament of the fire, and through the moderation of the degrees <note>alchemists categorized fire into four "degrees" of intensity, from a gentle lamp to a full blast-furnace</note> of the fire. And in this process, the **tinctures** <note>the potent essences or "souls" of metals capable of transforming them</note> are turned into one another.

For as it is said in the *Book of the 70 Precepts* <note>original: *Buch de 70. praeceptis*; likely the *Kitab al-Sab'in* attributed to Jabir ibn Hayyan</note>: Whoever knows how to turn gold into silver also knows how to turn silver into gold. And the *Rosary* <note>original: *Rosarius*; likely the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a cornerstone text of Western alchemy</note> says: One must turn the elements into one another—that is, in a circular fashion <note>original: *Cirkel weiß* (zirkelweise)</note>—which is the joining of the warm and moist with the cold and dry, through a subtle disposition and a wonderful joining. As **Morienus** <note>a legendary 7th-century hermit-alchemist</note> says: For air and water agree in their moisture, and earth and fire agree in their dryness. And for this reason, they are easily turned into one another, and more slowly separated from each other. However, fire and water, or earth and air, cannot be turned into one another unless the fire is first turned into air, and the earth is first turned into water, or vice-versa.

<summary>This page explains the alchemical "inversion" of elements, describing how substances must change states—from body to spirit and back—to achieve the Philosophers' Stone. It outlines the natural affinity between elements sharing common qualities like moisture or dryness.</summary>

# Laurentius Ventura

Therefore, if you turn the dry into the cold, and the cold into the moist, and the moist into the warm, you will have complete mastery of the elements. This separation does not happen through physical force, but is rather a transformation of the **tinctures** <term>tinctures: the potent liquid essences or "souls" of metals believed to have the power to transform base substances into gold</term> and natures. For this reason, it is said in the *Book of Saturn* <note>original: *lib. Saturni*</note>: **Azoth** <term>Azoth: a term for the "universal solvent" or the essential spirit of mercury, considered the beginning and end of the alchemical work</term> washes the impurity away from **Latona** <note>original: *Latona*; in alchemy, this refers to the "blackened" or impure matter that must be purified to reach the white stage of the Work</note>, and **Azoth** and **Latona** are always together and are never separated; indeed, they remain united at all times. But because of their many different colors, the **Philosophers** <note>a term alchemists used to refer to themselves and the ancient authorities of their craft</note> have called them by many different names.

In such a way, an artist must know the weight of the elements and the **limits of the tempering of the fire** <note>original: *terminos temperamenti ignis*; the precise control and duration of heat levels</note>, as **Master Bonus** <note>Petrus Bonus, a 14th-century alchemist known for his work *The New Pearl of Great Price*</note> says in Chapter 5. It is not that this weight is known to the artist through a physical scale; rather, he should know when all elements are present and appear visibly pure within a single element. At that point, nature has weighed all the other **elements** <note>original: *Elementa*</note> within that one single element according to the natural and true **proportion**. And therefore, if the artist does not know the designated time for the purification of these elements, he cannot possibly know their weight and composition, and consequently, he knows nothing at all. Thus it is said in the *Light of Lights* <note>original: *Lumine luminum*; a title of various medieval treatises, often attributed to the Persian physician Rhazes</note>: The weight shall never leave your memory. But by this opinion, the work is made to seem very difficult. Yet as far as the work of the **boiling** <note>original: *Kochung*; the slow, steady heating of the alchemical matter in a sealed vessel</note> is concerned, it is called "women's work," <note>a common alchemical phrase suggesting that once the substances are prepared, the process is as simple and patient as tending a kitchen fire or a laundry vat</note>

### Chapter 20.
## That in the governance of the stone there are not many various degrees of fire.

Some have thought that in the **governance** <term>governance: the careful management of heat intensity throughout the alchemical process</term> of the fire, various **degrees** <note>original: "Gradus"</note> must be administered according to the difference of time, in order to bring forth various effects, colors, and natures: and that the sayings of the philosophers make it appear as if they required such a thing. For **Pandulphus** in the **Assembly** <note>original: "Turba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, one of the oldest and most influential Latin alchemical texts, written as a transcript of a debate among ancient sages</note> says: Beware that you do not make a great fire before the time, and see to it that the fire itself be gentle to whiten the thing, until it be **coagulated** <term>coagulated: the process of a liquid substance thickening or becoming solid</term>. Therefore it appears that the fire should be increased a little after the **whitening** <note>original: "Weisse"; the *albedo* stage of the work where the matter turns white, signaling high purity</note>. Likewise, another philosopher in the **Assembly** says: One must burn the ore with the other part of the water, so that it simultaneously becomes soft in the water. But when the water has been turned into earth, then make the fire larger; and **Raymond** in *On the Terms* <note>original: "Raymundus de terminis"; likely referring to works attributed to Raymond Lully, a famous 13th-century polymath and alchemist</note>:

Therefore the **philosophers** <note>original: "Philosophi"; the historical masters of alchemy</note> have commanded us to govern the same gently until the **sulfur** <note>original: "Sulphur"; one of the three primary alchemical principles, representing the active, combustible soul of matter</note> becomes incombustible. > Construct a philosophical furnace, and therein kindle the **natural fire** <note>original Latin: "ignem phylicum," likely a corruption of "ignem physicum"</note>. 

For the **matter** <note>original: "Materi"</note> shall be made either of sheep’s dung or of oil-leaves <note>metaphorical terms for materials used to maintain a low, steady, and consistent heat over long periods</note>. This, however, is nothing other than that the fire may last equally during the burning, so long as the **whiteness** <note>the *albedo* stage, signaling the purification of the stone</note> remains well-strengthened within it, and you shall not find it ignited because of the fire burning out. And **Morienus** in the **Castrensi** <note>referring to the *Liber de compositione alchemiae*, an influential early Latin translation of Arabic alchemy</note> says: 
> When you have prepared the **unclean body** <note>original: "unreine Corpus"; the base metal or starting material before purification</note>, leave therein afterward also the fourth part of its **ferment** <term>ferment: a substance, often gold or silver, added to the alchemical matter to "leaven" it and direct its transformation toward the desired metal</term>, place it in the sun, and cook it; and its fire shall be gentle, and its days shall last with equal burning without ceasing, so that it becomes neither stronger nor smaller. 

Therefore **Bonellus** in the **Assembly** <note>original: "Turba," referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* or "Assembly of the Philosophers," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts</note> says: 
> If that which improves is not in the thing itself, then that which you seek will not come from it. 

For it is truly within it that it may be made better, provided it is not driven away with too much fire or with too much haste: and therefore patience and delay are necessary.

Hence **Zeno** <note>original: "Zinon"; an ancient philosopher cited in the *Turba Philosophorum*</note> says: 
> If one who enters into this art knew his own nature, he would certainly endure the length of the cooking with patience until he obtained his purpose therefrom through the grace of **GOD**. 

And **Morienus** says: 
> The artist should know the kindling of the fire, and the number of its days, and the weight and measure thereof.

From this it is now evident: that the fire shall remain equal until the end of the work. If, however, it is sometimes commanded that one should make a stronger or larger fire, this is not to be understood as a greater warmth, but rather as a matter of time. For the longer a thing remains or stands in the same warmth, the more it is transformed and changed by the action of the fire from one nature into another. Therefore, because it was previously wet, it shall afterwards be dry; and what was initially black or white, shall thereafter become **citrine** <term>citrine: a lemon-yellow color (citrinitas) representing the stage of transition between the white and red works</term> red, etc.

## Chapter 21.
## That the fire should always be gentle and steady.

But since there are many **degrees of fire** <note>original: "Gradus des Feuers"; alchemists traditionally recognized four degrees of heat, ranging from the warmth of a brooding hen to a full blast furnace</note>, one must now observe how great it should be, whether it should be strong or weak. To answer this: first, the fire should be mild and gentle. Thus the **Lilium** <note>likely referring to the *Lilium Alchimiae* (The Lily of Alchemy), a popular medieval text often attributed to Raymond Lully</note> says: 
> You should know that without warmth, nothing is ever born, and that great heat destroys, and that cold soon drives away the compound. 

But through a tempered fire, the body becomes lovely and suitable. For through a mild fire, the **destructive moisture** <note>original: "zerstörliche Feuchtigkeit"; the unstable, "accidental" humidity that prevents the matter from fixing and becoming permanent</note> is drawn out; for the **philosophers** <note>the historical masters of the alchemical tradition</note> all testify that they have found no other fire that draws out the destructive moisture than a gentle and mild one.
